I sense that the heat of dramatic tension will lie in Winston’s burgeoning discontent. It’s a great start. I’m enjoying the novel on its own terms, not as a classic but as a good story; that is, until Winston reveals himself to be a problematic character. For example, we learn of him: “He disliked nearly all women, and especially the young and pretty ones.” Whoa, wait a minute, Orwell. Winston’s views on women are, at first, despicable to the contemporary reader. He is the kind of character who can make me put a book down. When I was younger, that’s exactly what I would have done. But I’m a more seasoned reader now’, and I know the difference between a flawed character and a flawed story. And I remind myself that this is a dystopian novel, an idea of what society might look like if certain dark forces prevail. Orwell is suggesting misogyny is likely in a totalitarian society, and Winston is a product of that environment. Naturally, the women characters are also affected by totalitarianism. Under the Party’s rule, the sole purpose of marriage is to produce children. Katharine, Winston’s estranged wife, is diligently committed to that principle, but she despises the duty, and they remain childless. Julia, a twenty-six-year-old who works in the Fiction Department, takes the initiative to seduce Winston; unlike Katharine, she has reclaimed her sexuality as something more than a means to reproduce. Julia fervently believes the best way to rebel against the Party is by these small acts of individualism. That individualism is also on display in the tireless singing of the laundry woman in the courtyard behind Winston’s rented room. To Winston, her singing is delightful and brightens the dismal scene. Her ability to find joy in a mundane existence is deeply affecting to him, and he concludes from this joy that she must be beautiful. Luckily for us, Winston evolves as his love for Julia grows. Though he struggles with sincere emotion, because for so many years the Party has deprived its citizens of passion, he still manages to fall in love with her. By reconnecting him to his suppressed emotions, Julia teaches him there is a part of himself that the Party cannot reach. At this point I feel glad I’ve continued with the story. Orwell is suggesting that love and artistic beauty can act as healing forces in a totalitarian state. I think of my own love for literature, the ways in which my lifelong passion for reading has healed me on many occasions. I think of my love for family, friends, and community, and I am invested in the story again. I am turning pages. I wouldn’t say that I identify with these themes of human connection because they are universal. I am of the generation that pushed back against notions of the universal., especially when they weren’t universal at all and applied only to a particular kind of experience. I am a Black female reader, and these identifiers are primary points of entry into any text for me. Not that every book I love must contain a character who looks or thinks like me; I have learned to do what many readers on the margins have learned to do: read around the margins. In other words, I examine the contours of a novel like an outline that I can trace, to find connection to the story even in the tiniest details. And Orwell’s nods to the possibilities of love and pleasure are an outline I can trace over and over. That sliver of connection can be difficult for someone like me to find in a novel that does not speak much to race and ethnicity at all. In Oceania, there is supposedly no racism. “Nor is there any racial discrimination, or any marked domination of one province by another. Jews. Negroes, South Americans of pure Indian blood are to be found in the highest ranks of the Party, and administrators of any area are always drawn from the inhabitants of that area. In no part of Oceania do the inhabitants have the feeling they are a colonial population ruled from a distant capital.” When I read this, I cannot help but think of Ralph Ellison’s Invisible Man and its publication in the United States just a year after 1984 was published in Britain. In Ellison’s novel, whites don’t see Blacks, while in Orwell’s novel, there are no Black characters at all. As a contemporary reader I find myself pausing again. It is plausible that there is no racism and colonialism in Orwell’s world since the totalitarian government has erased and rewritten history numerous times in an effort to portray the government in a positive light. But Orwell suggests it is impossible to completely ignore these “secret” histories. In his first diary entry at the beginning of the novel, Winston writes of seeing a war film in which a woman who is possibly a “jewess” sits among refugees in a lifeboat—a possible reference to Holocaust refugees. In a 1945 essay. “Antisemitism in Britain.” Orwell frankly criticizes antisemitism among his British contemporaries, but in other documents he is guilty of the very antisemitic remarks that he disapprovingly notes in others. Despite these contradictions. I am willing to accept that Orwell wants to center other concerns, and I dip back into Winston’s world. As a storyteller. Orwell provides a satisfying ending, and though I am finished. I find myself flipping back through the book, rereading passages. This is the kind of book that one must digest, a book that I want to discuss with someone. I may not physically be in the classroom, but I am. A classroom of my own making.
